passages.text: At dawn Peter came in and said, “Let Clement, his mother Mattidia, and my wife sit together in the carriage.” And so it was done. As we set out on the road toward Balaneae, my mother asked me how my father was doing. I said, “He went away in search of you and my twin brothers, Faustinus and Faustinianus, and cannot be found. I think he has most likely died, either suffering shipwreck, meeting disaster on the road, or wasting away with grief.” When she heard this, she became tearful and sighed in sorrow. Yet her joy at finding me somewhat softened the grief the recollection brought. We arrived at Balaneae. On the following day we came to Paltus, and from there to Gabala; on the next we arrived at Laodicea. There, before the gates, Nicetas and Aquila met us, embraced us with kisses, and led us to our lodging. Seeing that it was a fine, large city, Peter said, “It is worthwhile to stay here for some days, for generally a large population is better able to produce the people being sought.” Nicetas and Aquila asked me who this unfamiliar woman was. I said, “My mother, whom God granted me to recognize through my master Peter.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: This qualifies the narrator’s inference, not verified knowledge of death. “For the most part” is more literal but less natural here.
Peter’s generalization about a crowd can refer to missing persons in this recognition narrative; it can also mean the people sought for his mission. The main text does not specify which group.
κύριος here is a respectful human title for Peter, not an identification with the divine Lord. “My lord Peter” is the more formal alternative.

passages.text: After I said this, Peter gave them a summary of everything: how, as soon as they had gone ahead, I, Clement, had told him about my family; about my mother’s departure with her twin children on the fabricated pretext of the dream; and also about my father’s departure to search for her. Then he told how he himself, Peter, after hearing these things, went onto the island, encountered the woman, saw her begging, and asked the reason for her begging. He learned her family background, her way of life, the fabricated dream, and the children’s names—mine, the one left with my father, and those of the twin children who traveled with her—and how they were supposed to have died in the depths.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἐν βυθῷ ὑπενοεῖτο τεθνηκέναι
lexical_decisions.chosen: and how they were supposed to have died in the depths
lexical_decisions.rationale: The subject of the infinitive is unexpressed and the finite verb singular can be impersonal. The main text links the supposed death to the twin children just named; a reference to the mother as one presumed dead is also possible. The supposition is not presented as an actual death.

passages.text: After Peter had related these things in summary, Nicetas and Aquila were astounded and said, “Master and Lord of all, is this true, or is it a dream?” Peter said, “If we are not asleep, it is true.” After a short pause for thought, they said, “We are Faustinus and Faustinianus. From the beginning of your account, we looked at one another and made many conjectures about ourselves, wondering whether what was being said might not concern us, while reflecting that many similar things happen in life. That is why we kept silent, our hearts pounding. But when we looked to the end of the account and saw that what was being said concerned us, then we disclosed who we were.” Saying this, they went in to their mother in tears, found her sleeping, and wanted to embrace her at once. But Peter stopped them, saying, “Let me bring you in and present you to your mother, so that the great sudden joy does not drive her out of her senses, since she is asleep and her spirit is occupied by sleep.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἆρά γε, δέσποτα καὶ κύριε τῶν ἁπάντων
lexical_decisions.rationale: The address is retained without adding an explicit “God”; the wording can be an exclamation addressed to the universal divine ruler within the dialogue. It is not silently made an assertion that Peter rules everything.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μὴ ἄρα οὐχ ἡμῖν διαφέρει τὰ λεγόμενα
lexical_decisions.chosen: wondering whether what was being said might not concern us
lexical_decisions.rationale: The nested interrogative/negative particles convey their hesitant recognition. The English “might not” keeps the negated question without imposing a uniquely certain expected answer.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὸ πνεῦμα ὑπὸ τοῦ ὕπνου ἀπησχολημένον
lexical_decisions.chosen: her spirit is occupied by sleep
lexical_decisions.rationale: πνεῦμα may be spirit or the animating breath; no modern theory of unconsciousness is added.

passages.text: When she had had enough sleep and awakened, Peter began speaking with my mother about reverence for God, saying first, “Woman, I want you to know the way of life of our religion. We worship one God, who made the world you see, and we keep his law. Its first requirements include worshiping him alone, treating his name as holy, honoring parents, being chaste, and living pleasantly. In addition, since we do not live without distinctions, we do not partake of the nations’ table; indeed, we cannot even dine with them, because they live impurely. But whenever we persuade them to think and do what belongs to the truth, and baptize them with a certain thrice-blessed invocation, then we gather at table with them. Even if someone happens to be a father, mother, wife, child, brother, or anyone else for whom one has natural affection, we cannot dare to dine with that person: we do this as a distinctive religious practice. So do not regard your son’s not dining with you as an insult, until you think and do the same things as he does.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied adjective’s adverbial form refers to pleasant living; it is not changed to a conjectural “uprightly” or made a command to indulgence.
The singular description of a naming or invocation is retained; no specific baptismal formula or persons are supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: we do this as a distinctive religious practice
lexical_decisions.rationale: The expression can also be understood as “we do this especially on religious grounds.” The main wording keeps the religious distinction and does not present the rule as a universal modern obligation.

passages.text: When she heard this, she said, “What, then, prevents me from being baptized today? Even before seeing you, I turned away from the so-called gods, reasoning that, though I sacrificed much to them nearly every day, they did not stand by me in my need. And what need is there even to speak about adultery? Even when I was rich, luxury did not deceive me into it; nor has the poverty that followed been able to force me into it. I have held fast to chastity as the greatest beauty, and on its account I came into such distress. Nor do I think you are unaware, my master Peter, that greater desire comes from good spirits. Therefore, having remained chaste in good spirits, I do not sell myself to pleasures in dejection. But do not suppose that my soul is now free of suffering, though it has received some consolation through recognizing Clement. For the grief over my two children comes back in and dims even that small joy. For what grieves us is not so much the in [I will exhort, for, about them, that these perished alongside in the sea; in the sea they perished, but not that as much as the apart from the divine, toward God, reveren-; in addition to these outside the walls, religion, -ce, to be destroyed together with the souls; destroyed away from God, the bodies and their bodies with them; they lost souls]. But their father, my husband, as I learned from Clement, went away to search both for me and for our sons and has been missing for so many years; he has certainly died. For the poor man loved me because of chastity and was fond of his children. Therefore, deprived of all of us, whom he loved above everything, the old man perished from the greatest despondency.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The term concerns cheerfulness, confidence, or favorable circumstances. “Prosperity” is contextually possible given the preceding wealth, but the main text retains its contrast with δυσθυμία, dejection.
The verb can mean give over or sell. The contextual prospect of sexual conduct under poverty supports “sell”; “give myself over” remains possible.

source_issues.source_quote: λυπεῖ γὰρ ἡμᾶς οὐ τοσοῦτον τὸ ἐν παραινέσω μὲν γὰρ περὶ αὐτῶν ὅτι ἐν τῇ θαλάσσῃ τούτους παραπολέσθαι, θαλάσσῃ διεφώνησαν, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὅτι ὅσον τὸ χωρὶς τῆς θείας εἰς θεὸν εὐσε- πρὸς τούτοις ἐκτὸς τειχῶν θρησκείας βείας διαφθαρῆναι μετά γε τῶν ψυχῶν θεοῦ φθαρέντες τὰ σώματα καὶ τὰς αὐτοῖς καὶ τὰ σώματα. ψυχὰς ἀπώλοντο.
source_issues.issue: The supplied consecutive wording cannot currently be given a coherent, complete grammatical translation. It includes disrupted phrases, a split εὐσε- ... βείας, and wording that could reflect parallel or interleaved formulations, but that is not established here as an OCR error or permission to omit words. The main text visibly brackets an attempted literal representation of all fragments rather than silently selecting a coherent subset. That bracketed passage is not publication-ready. The confirmed print’s layout or intended sequence must be clarified, or a defensible interpretation accounting for every surviving form must be established independently.

passages.text: While my mother was saying this, the boys, who were listening as Peter had advised, could no longer contain themselves. They stood up and embraced her, weeping abundantly and covering her with kisses. She said, “What does this mean?” Peter answered, “Woman, steady your mind courageously, so that you may enjoy your children. These are your sons Faustinus and Faustinianus, whom you said had died in the depths. How they are alive, after dying in your presence on that dreadful night, and how one of them is now called Nicetas and the other Aquila, they themselves will be able to tell you. We too have to learn it along with you.” When Peter said this, my mother was so overjoyed that she nearly died from faintness. When we revived her, she sat down, came to herself, and said, “My longed-for children, please tell us what happened to you after that terrible night.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: Peter echoes her belief about the shipwreck rather than independently asserting an actual death and resurrection. “Having died as far as you were concerned” is a contextual alternative; the main text keeps the sharper surviving wording.

passages.text: Nicetas, henceforth Faustinus, began to speak: “That very night, when the ship was breaking apart, as you know, some men who were not afraid to plunder in the depths picked us up and put us in a boat. Rowing, they took us sometimes along the shore and sometimes sent for provisions, bringing us to Strato’s Caesarea. There, by hunger, fear, and blows, though we were weeping, they managed to sell us, after also changing our names so that we would not rashly say anything they did not want said. A very distinguished woman named Justa, a convert to the Jews, bought us, kept us in the place of children, and diligently educated us in every branch of Greek learning. As we grew up and became sensible, we loved the religion and applied ourselves to learning, so that in discussions with the other nations we could expose their error. We also mastered the philosophers’ teachings, especially the most godless—I mean those of Epicurus and Pyrrho—so that we could refute them more effectively.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: kept us in the place of children
lexical_decisions.rationale: Their purchase and subsequent treatment are both retained. The text does not explicitly describe a legal adoption or manumission.
The superlative belongs to the narrator’s evaluation of the philosophers, not an added evaluation by the translator.

passages.text: “Having become almost companions from childhood with a certain magician, Simon, we came close to being deceived through friendship. There is an account about a certain man: when he appears in kingship, the [ὁ ... ων] of those who have revered God will be able to live immortally and without pain. But these things, mother, will be explained to you more precisely at the proper time. Just when we were about to be deceived by Simon, a companion of our master Peter, called Zacchaeus, took us in and warned us not to be deceived by the magician. When Peter arrived, he brought us to him, so that, by giving us full assurance, he might persuade us about the matters pertaining to reverence for God. Therefore, mother, we also pray that you may share in the good things we have been granted, so that we may partake of salt and table together. This, then, mother, is why you thought we had died: on that dreadful night pirates carried us off on the open sea, while you supposed we had perished.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase may indicate appearing in royal rule or within a kingdom; the main text chooses the former without supplying a realm or identifying the man.
The concrete shared-meal language is retained rather than reduced to social friendship.

source_issues.issue: The edition prints a three-dot gap with surviving ὁ and ων around it. These are retained literally as [ὁ ... ων], without restoring a person, group, or participle. The surrounding phrase is therefore visibly incomplete; the missing content has not been recovered.

passages.text: After Faustinus said this, our mother fell at Peter’s feet, begging and requesting that he send for her hostess and baptize both her and the hostess immediately. “Let there be no day,” she said, “from the time I have recovered my own children, on which I am deprived of dining with them.” When we too joined our mother in pleading for this, Peter said, “What do you think? Am I alone unfeeling, because I do not want you to dine with your mother by baptizing her today? But she must fast at least one day before being baptized. Even this is because she simply uttered a statement on her own behalf that I recognized as a sufficient expression of her faith; otherwise she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: she needs many days to be weaned from Greek religion
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb denotes being de-Hellenized, here in a discussion of religious preparation, not renouncing Greek language or ethnicity. “To be freed from pagan practice” is an alternative but less transparent about the Greek category.

passages.text: I said, “Tell us what statement she uttered that revealed her faith.” Peter said, “Her request that the hostess who had been her benefactor be baptized with her. She would not have asked for this to be given to the woman she loved unless she herself had first come to regard the gift of baptism as something great. Therefore I condemn many people when, after being baptized and saying that they believe, they do nothing worthy of faith and do not urge even those they love—I mean their wives, sons, or friends—to this. For if they have believed that God grants eternal life at baptism together with good deeds, they would without delay have urged those they loved to be baptized. But one of you will say, ‘They love them and care for them.’ This is foolish. Why, then, when they see them ill, being led away to death, or suffering other terrible things, do they lament and pity them? In the same way, if they had believed that eternal fire awaits those who do not worship God, they would not have stopped admonishing them, or, when they saw them disobedient, grieving over them as unbelievers, being fully assured of the punishment against them. Now, then, I will send for the hostess and question her whether she chooses to love the law conveyed through us, and then we will do what is required accordingly.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ζωὴν αἰώνιον σὺν ἔργοις καλοῖς δωρεῖσθαι τὸν θεὸν ἐπὶ τῷ βαπτίσματι
lexical_decisions.chosen: God grants eternal life at baptism together with good deeds
lexical_decisions.rationale: σὺν ἔργοις καλοῖς is preserved alongside baptism; it can qualify the granting as connected with good works or characterize the life/gift together with them. The text’s combination is not recast as baptism only symbolizing or independently causing salvation.
εὔηθες can mean simple or naive as well as foolish; here it challenges the adequacy of an objection, not their loved ones’ intelligence.

passages.text: “Since your mother approaches baptism with faith, let her fast at least one day before baptism.” But she swore, “For two of the days that have passed, while telling the woman about the recognition, I was unable to partake of food because of my great joy, except for a little water yesterday alone.” Peter’s wife testified to her oath, saying, “She has indeed tasted nothing.” Aquila—or rather, henceforth Faustinianus—said, “Then nothing prevents her from being baptized.” Peter laughed and answered, “But this is not a baptismal fast, since it did not take place for that purpose.” Faustinus answered, “Perhaps, then, God, wishing our mother not to be separated from the table for even one day after recognizing us, arranged the fast beforehand. For just as she remained chaste in ignorance, doing what accords with the truth, so perhaps God has now arranged for her to fast a day beforehand, in ignorance, for the sake of the true baptism, so that from the very first day of recognizing us she may partake of salt with us.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: since it did not take place for that purpose
lexical_decisions.rationale: The loose ἤ-clause is read as giving the qualification that the earlier abstention was not for baptism. “Unless it took place for that purpose” is an alternative way of expressing the criterion, but the main text links it to the actual earlier non-baptismal fast.
The feminine day is understood from the surrounding fasting discussion; no longer duration is added.

passages.text: Peter said, “Let not evil overcome us by finding a pretext in providence and a mother’s affection. Rather, let you and I with you endure today, and tomorrow she will be baptized. Indeed, the hour of today is not suitable for baptism.” And we all agreed together that it should be done this way.

lexical_decisions.rationale: This can be abstract badness or personified evil. The main text leaves the personification without explicitly naming a devil.

lexical_decisions.chosen: let you and I with you endure today
lexical_decisions.rationale: The day and waiting are expressed; no new independent baptismal requirement is supplied.

passages.text: That very evening we all enjoyed Peter’s teaching. From the occasion provided by our mother, he showed us why the outcomes of chastity are good, whereas those of adultery, being grievous, naturally bring destruction upon an entire family, if not quickly, then at least eventually. “Chastity,” he said, “is so pleasing to God that even to those who are in error he assigns some small favor for it in the present life. For salvation there is given only to those who have been baptized because of their hope in him and who act righteously with chastity. You have seen this happen in your mother’s case—I mean the good outcomes. Perhaps, had she committed adultery, she would have been killed. Therefore, because she remained chaste, God had mercy on her, averted the murder directed against her, and restored the children who had been taken away.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: γένος may also mean lineage or kind; the family-recognition narrative supports the family sense here.
The contrast with the present life points beyond this life; the English retains the deictic “there” instead of adding a named place.

passages.text: “But perhaps someone will say, ‘How many have perished because of chastity?’ I say it was because of insensibility. For a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor, must immediately flee association with him as she would a blazing fire or a rabid dog. This is what your mother did, truly loving the beauty of chastity. Therefore she was preserved and received with us the knowledge of the eternal kingdom. A woman who wants to remain chaste must know that, envied by evil, she has many who plot against her under the pretext of love. Yet by the single resolve to remain chaste, continuing honorable and gaining victory over them all, she will be able to be saved. For the prophet said that, even if someone does every good thing, for the single sin of committing adultery one must be punished.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν αἰσθανομένην ἢ γενομένου τινὸς ἐραστοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: a woman who becomes aware, or who finds that someone has become a suitor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed disjunction ἤ is retained as two ways the danger becomes apparent, the second originally expressed through a genitive absolute. “A woman who notices that someone has become a lover” is smoother but suppresses the printed disjunction. ἐραστής here is a pursuing lover or suitor, not necessarily someone whose advances have been accepted.
The agent can be personified evil or human wickedness; no particular demon or person is supplied.

passages.text: “The chaste woman, doing God’s will, becomes a good reminder of his first creation: God, being one, created one woman for one man. She remains still more chaste if she does not forget the creation, foresees the punishment, and is not unaware of the loss of eternal good things. The chaste woman, delighting in those who wish to be saved, is a reverent example to those who revere God, for she is a rule of good living. The woman who wishes to remain chaste cuts off occasions for abuse. But if she is abused without giving an occasion, as by an enemy, God blesses and vindicates her. The chaste woman longs for God, loves God, delights God, glorifies God; she gives people no occasion for abuse. The chaste woman perfumes the assembly with good honor and glorifies it by her dignity. She is also the teachers’ praise and works alongside them as they exercise chastity.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The woman embodies a norm or rule of good living; she is not made a new written statute.
The noun denotes the gathered community, not specifically its building or an institution of a later era.

lexical_decisions.chosen: works alongside them as they exercise chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: σωφρονοῦσι agrees with the teachers as a dative participle. It can also imply her collaboration with them in fostering chastity; the main reading keeps their own chastity explicit.

passages.text: “The chaste woman adorns herself for the Son of God as for a bridegroom, clothed in the honorable light. Her beauty is the good order within her soul. She breathes a perfume: her good reputation. She is clothed in beautiful head-coverings, modesty, and wears precious pearls, the words that teach chastity. She is white when her understanding has been made radiant. She looks in a beautiful mirror, gazing upon God. She uses beautiful adornment, instructing her soul through fear toward God. Beautiful is the woman who is not shackled with gold but freed from desires for temporary things. The chaste woman is greatly desired by a great king; she is betrothed to him, kept for him, loved by him. The chaste woman gives no occasion for being desired except by her own husband. The chaste woman is distressed when desired by another. The chaste woman loves her husband inwardly, kisses him affectionately, flatters him, pleases him, serves him, and obeys him in everything except disobeying God. For the woman who obeys God is chaste in soul and pure in body even without guards.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λευκὴ δὲ τυγχάνει, ὅταν τὰς φρένας ᾖ λελαμπτρυμμένη
lexical_decisions.chosen: She is white when her understanding has been made radiant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The whiteness is part of the preceding apparel/adornment imagery and is explicitly connected to the mind. It is not rendered as a claim about skin color.
ἐνδιαθέτως marks inward disposition or sincere affection. “From the heart” is an idiomatic alternative.

The verb is stronger than occasional assistance and can denote servile service. The hierarchical marital claim remains the ancient speaker’s; it is not softened into equal partnership or supplemented with a claim of legal ownership.

passages.text: “Foolish, then, is every man who separates his own wife from fear of God. For the woman who does not fear God does not fear her husband either. If she does not fear God, who sees invisible things, how will she keep her invisible choice chaste? And how will she remain chaste if she does not come to hear the words that teach chastity? How could she receive admonition? How will she remain chaste without guards if she is not taught about God’s coming judgment and is not fully assured of the eternal loss that follows a little pleasure? Therefore, on the contrary, compel her, even unwilling, always to attend the discourse that teaches chastity; coax her.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase concerns an inward decision or intention not visible to people. “Her inward will” is another rendering.
The coercive force of ἀνάγκασον, compel, and the wife’s unwillingness are both retained as the speaker’s instruction, not softened to a consensual invitation.
The imperative can mean flatter or cajole; the persuasion does not erase the preceding command to compel.

passages.text: “Much better still, if you lead her by the hand and come, so that you too may become chaste. For you will wish to become chaste so that you may know the outcome of honorable marriage—and you will not shrink back if you love, I mean, becoming a father, loving your own children, and being loved by your own children. A man who wants a chaste wife is himself chaste. He renders the goodwill he owes, eats with her, is with her, comes with her to the discourse that teaches chastity, does not grieve her, does not quarrel without cause, does not make himself hateful, and provides whatever good things he can. What he does not have, he makes up for with affectionate persuasion. The chaste woman does not wait to be coaxed; she recognizes her husband as master, bears his poverty when he is poor, goes hungry with him when he is hungry, travels away with him when he travels away, comforts him when he is distressed, and, even if she has a larger dowry, submits as though she had nothing. The husband, even if his wife is poor, should consider her chastity a great dowry. The chaste woman uses a sufficient amount of food and drink, so that, when her body has grown fat, she is not dragged down in her soul by its weight toward unlawful desires. Moreover, she does not spend time alone with young men and is suspicious of old men. She rejects disorderly laughter; assigning herself to God alone, she does not stumble. She delights in hearing honorable words and rejects those not spoken for chastity.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The phrase denotes owed goodwill or benevolence; a specifically sexual marital duty can be contextually heard but is not named.
The same root as “coax” can mean flattery or cajoling. Here it makes up for absent material goods; the main text does not change it into financial compensation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: she is not dragged down in her soul
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive is preserved with τὴν ψυχήν as accusative of respect. The isolated dot before τὴν is printed punctuation, not a multi-dot lacuna; it is not represented as missing wording.

passages.text: “God is witness: one adultery is many murders. And the dreadful thing is that the terrifying and impious nature of its murders is not seen. For when blood has been shed, a dead body lies there, and the horror of the calamity shocks everyone. But adultery’s murders of the soul, though more fearful, because people do not see them, give those who dare an unhesitating impulse. Know, human being, whose breath you have for life, and you will certainly not want it to be defiled. God’s breath is defiled by adultery alone, and for this reason it brings the one who defiled it into fire: it hastens to hand the offender over to eternal punishment.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: The compressed equation and its force are preserved as the speaker’s metaphorical claim about souls, not reduced to merely causing unhappiness.
The exclusivity is explicit and retained, without harmonizing it with broader accounts of sin.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτὴ τὸν μιάναντα εἰς πῦρ καταστᾷ
lexical_decisions.chosen: it brings the one who defiled it into fire
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine pronoun refers grammatically to God’s breath. It is not silently replaced by a different subject such as God or the sinner.

passages.text: As Peter was saying this, he saw the good and chaste Mattidia weeping for joy. Thinking that she had become sorrowful at the recollection of what had happened, he said, “Take courage, woman. While many have suffered many evils because of adultery, you have not suffered because of chastity, and for this reason you did not die. And even if you had died, you would have had your soul saved. Did you leave your homeland, Rome, because of chastity? Yet through that occasion you found truth, the diadem of the everlasting kingdom. Have you been in danger in the depths? Yet you did not die, and if you had died, the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity, toward your soul’s salvation. Were you separated from your children? For a little while: coming from legitimate seed, they have been found among better things. Did you beg for food while starving? Yet you did not defile your body through prostitution. Did you torment your body? Yet you saved your soul. Did you flee an adulterer so as not to defile your husband’s bed? Yet, because of chastity, God, who knows of your flight, will fill the husband’s place. Were you grieved and left alone, separated for a little while from husband and children? Yet you were bound to leave them all at death’s appointed time. Better that you were separated willingly because of chastity than that, later, unwillingly, you should perish in those very sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you have not suffered because of chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The negative is retained, though the surrounding account relates her hardships to protecting chastity. It can contrast the true cause of suffering with its occasion, but the translation does not rewrite it as “you suffered because of chastity.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: αὐτός σοι ὁ βυθὸς διὰ σωφροσύνην θνησκούσῃ βάπτισμα ἐγίνετο
lexical_decisions.chosen: the depths themselves would have become baptism for you, dying for chastity
lexical_decisions.rationale: The conditional claim of baptism through death for chastity is explicitly the speaker’s; no sacramental qualification is inserted to reconcile it with the following teaching.
The language concerns the children’s origin from a legitimate union. The main text retains seed imagery and does not add a biological or doctrinal theory.
The promised replacement or fulfillment of the husband’s place is retained; its precise nature is not defined as sexual or institutional.

passages.text: “So it is much better for the first things to be distressing. Even when they are present, the hope that they will pass keeps them from causing too much sorrow, and expectation of something better even gives joy. Above all, I want you to know how greatly chastity pleases God. The chaste woman is God’s choice, God’s delight, God’s glory, God’s child. Chastity is so great a good. If it were not the law that not even a righteous person may enter God’s kingdom unbaptized, perhaps those among the nations who are in error could have been saved through chastity alone. That is why I am greatly disheartened about those who remain chaste in error: having chosen chastity without good hope, they are hesitant about being baptized. Therefore they are not saved, because God’s decree is established that an unbaptized person must not enter his kingdom.” After he had said these things and still more, we turned to sleep.

lexical_decisions.chosen: not even a righteous person ... unbaptized
lexical_decisions.rationale: The emphatic exclusion of even a righteous unbaptized person is retained, rather than interpreting δίκαιον impersonally as “it is not right.”
This describes the chaste people still in error; it is not turned into an assertion that they have already received the speaker’s hope of salvation.
